title: Blood Composition & Hematopoiesis
summary: What blood is made of and how the bone marrow continuously builds every blood cell from stem cells.

lessons.title: What Blood Is Made Of: Plasma, Cells & Platelets

levels.kid:
Blood is like a busy river flowing through tubes all over your body. If you put blood in a special spinning machine, it separates into layers, a bit like a smoothie left on the counter.

- On top is **plasma**, a yellow liquid. It is mostly water, and it carries food, salts and messages around your body.
- At the bottom are **red blood cells**. They are tiny delivery trucks that carry oxygen from your lungs to every part of you.
- In a thin white middle layer are **white blood cells**, the guards that fight germs, and **platelets**, tiny pieces that rush to a cut and make a plug.

All these blood cells are made inside your bones, in a soft, spongy stuff called **marrow**. Your body makes millions of new ones every second!
levels.hs:
An adult has about 5 liters of blood, roughly 7% of body weight. If you spin a tube of blood in a centrifuge, it separates into three layers:

- **Plasma** (about 55%): the pale yellow liquid on top. It is about 92% water, plus proteins, salts (electrolytes), glucose, hormones and wastes like urea. The most abundant protein, **albumin**, keeps water inside blood vessels.
- **Buffy coat** (under 1%): a thin whitish band of **white blood cells** and **platelets**.
- **Red blood cells** (about 45%): packed at the bottom. This percentage is called the **hematocrit**.

The cells:
- **Red blood cells (erythrocytes)** are filled with **hemoglobin**, the protein that carries oxygen. They have no nucleus and live about 120 days.
- **White blood cells (leukocytes)** defend against infection. The most common type is the **neutrophil**, a bacteria-eating cell.
- **Platelets (thrombocytes)** are not whole cells. They are fragments that break off giant marrow cells called **megakaryocytes**, and they help form clots.

If blood is allowed to clot, the leftover liquid is called **serum**. Serum is plasma minus the clotting proteins, such as **fibrinogen**.

Real example: the most common blood test, the **complete blood count (CBC)**, measures exactly these things: red cell count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, white cell count and platelet count.
levels.college:
Blood is a fluid connective tissue: **formed elements** suspended in **plasma**. It transports gases, nutrients, hormones and heat; buffers pH (normally 7.35 to 7.45); defends against pathogens; and seals injuries.

**Plasma** (about 55% of volume) is about 92% water and 7% protein. **Albumin** generates most of the plasma **oncotic pressure** (about 25 mmHg), holding fluid in capillaries and carrying hydrophobic molecules. Globulins (including antibodies) and **fibrinogen** make up most of the rest. Plasma osmolality is held near 285 to 295 mOsm/kg, mainly by sodium. **Serum** is the fluid left after clotting, so it lacks fibrinogen and consumed clotting factors.

**Red blood cells** (about 4 to 6 million per microliter) are biconcave discs about 7 to 8 micrometers wide, giving a large surface area and the flexibility to squeeze through capillaries narrower than themselves. Mature RBCs have **no nucleus and no mitochondria**. They make ATP by anaerobic glycolysis, so they do not consume the oxygen they carry. Each lives about 120 days before the spleen and liver remove it.

**White blood cells** (about 4,000 to 11,000 per microliter). A typical differential:
- Neutrophils 50 to 70%
- Lymphocytes 20 to 40%
- Monocytes 2 to 8%
- Eosinophils 1 to 4%
- Basophils under 1%
(Mnemonic: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas.)

**Platelets** (about 150,000 to 450,000 per microliter) are anucleate fragments 2 to 3 micrometers across, shed from **megakaryocytes**. They survive about 8 to 10 days, and roughly one-third are held in the spleen at any moment.

**Hematocrit** reflects a ratio, not an absolute amount. It falls if plasma expands, as in pregnancy, and rises if plasma shrinks, as in dehydration.

**Lab tubes matter.** A CBC uses an EDTA tube, which chelates calcium to prevent clotting. Coagulation tests use citrate, and serum chemistry uses a clot-activator tube. The marrow replaces losses on an enormous scale: about 200 billion red cells and around 100 billion each of neutrophils and platelets every day.
levels.phd:
By number, blood dominates the body. Sender, Fuchs and Milo (2016) estimated about 30 trillion human cells in a reference adult, of which roughly 25 trillion (about 84%) are erythrocytes. By mass, however, red cells are a minority of body cell mass, because they are tiny compared with muscle fibers and adipocytes.

**Rheology.** Whole blood is a non-Newtonian, shear-thinning fluid. At low shear, red cells stack into rouleaux, a process promoted by fibrinogen, and viscosity rises. Viscosity climbs steeply with hematocrit, while oxygen-carrying capacity rises linearly with it. Oxygen delivery is therefore thought to peak near a hematocrit of about 40 to 45%, though the optimum depends on vessel geometry and flow. Two classic observations shape microvascular flow:
- The **Fåhræus effect**: tube hematocrit in narrow vessels is lower than discharge hematocrit, because cells travel faster than the plasma near the wall.
- The **Fåhræus–Lindqvist effect**: apparent viscosity falls in tubes narrower than about 0.3 mm, because deformable red cells migrate toward the axis and leave a low-viscosity, cell-free plasma layer at the wall.

RBC deformability depends on the spectrin–actin membrane skeleton and on a high surface-to-volume ratio. Losing either property shortens red cell survival.

**Counting.** Wallace Coulter's impedance principle, patented in the early 1950s, sizes cells as they pass through an aperture and disturb an electric current. It transformed hematology from manual hemocytometer counts into the automated CBC.

**Pools and kinetics.** About half of intravascular neutrophils are marginated along endothelium, mainly in the lungs, spleen and liver. Epinephrine and glucocorticoids demarginate them and raise the measured count within hours, without any new marrow production. Neutrophil lifespan is debated. The classic estimate of a circulating half-life of about 7 hours was challenged by Pillay and colleagues (2010), whose in vivo deuterium labeling suggested about 5.4 days. Tak and colleagues (2013) re-analyzed the labeling approach and argued for a circulating lifespan under a day.

**Serum vs plasma.** Platelets and leukocytes release intracellular contents during in vitro clotting. Serum potassium therefore normally exceeds plasma potassium slightly, and the gap widens with marked thrombocytosis. This produces **pseudohyperkalemia**, with no corresponding ECG changes.
levels.expert:
Most errors in interpreting blood composition are pre-analytical or physiological, not pathological. Some clinically important traps:

- **EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia** (seen in roughly 0.1% of samples): naturally occurring antibodies that recognize platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa when EDTA chelates calcium, causing platelets to aggregate after the blood is drawn. The analyzer reports a low count in a patient who is not bleeding. Look for platelet clumps on the smear and repeat the count in a citrate tube before canceling a procedure or transfusing.
- **Cold agglutinins** cause red cells to clump at room temperature. The result is a falsely low RBC count, a spuriously high MCV and an impossible MCHC. Warming the sample corrects it.
- **Contaminated draws**: blood taken downstream of (proximal to) a running IV infusion dilutes every cell line. Hemolysis during collection falsely raises potassium and LDH.
- **Acute hemorrhage**: whole blood is lost in proportion, so hemoglobin and hematocrit can look reassuring at first. They fall over hours as interstitial fluid and IV crystalloid refill the plasma volume. Judge early bleeding by hemodynamics, not by a single hemoglobin value.
- **Dilution versus true change**: in pregnancy, plasma volume expands by about 40 to 50% while red cell mass rises less, producing a physiological dilutional anemia. Altitude, smoking and androgens raise red cell mass.

**Reference intervals are population-dependent.** Many people of African and Middle Eastern ancestry carry the Duffy-null genotype (ACKR1). They have lower baseline neutrophil counts, now termed **Duffy-null associated neutrophil count**, without increased infection risk. Applying standard cutoffs has led to unnecessary marrow biopsies and to exclusion from clinical trials.

**For neurosurgery**, blood composition interacts with the brain directly. Hyperviscosity, for example in polycythemia or very high paraprotein levels, impairs cerebral microcirculation. Perioperative hemodilution shifts both oxygen content and viscosity.

**Recent advances and open questions.** Modern analyzers combine impedance with flow cytometry and fluorescence to report reticulocyte hemoglobin and the immature platelet fraction. Plasma is now mined as a diagnostic fluid: most circulating cell-free DNA comes from hematopoietic cells, which matters when interpreting liquid biopsies. Large-scale plasma proteomics is mapping thousands of proteins as disease markers. How to set individualized rather than population reference ranges remains unresolved.

keyPoints: Blood is about 55% plasma, under 1% buffy coat and about 45% red cells (the hematocrit)
Plasma is mostly water; albumin holds fluid in vessels; serum is plasma without clotting proteins
Red cells have no nucleus or mitochondria, carry oxygen in hemoglobin and live about 120 days
Neutrophils are the most common white cell (Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas)
Platelets are megakaryocyte fragments that live about 8 to 10 days
Lab artifacts and dilution can fake abnormal counts: always interpret in context

test.q: About what percentage of normal blood volume is plasma?
test.explain: Plasma makes up about 55% of blood. Red cells make up most of the rest (about 45%), and the buffy coat is under 1%.

test.q: After centrifugation, the thin whitish buffy coat contains mainly:
test.explain: The buffy coat is the band of leukocytes and platelets between the plasma and the packed red cells. Proteins and electrolytes stay dissolved in the plasma.

test.q: Which white blood cell is most abundant in a typical adult's blood?
test.explain: Neutrophils make up about 50 to 70% of white cells. Lymphocytes come second at about 20 to 40%.

test.q: What are platelets?
test.explain: Platelets are anucleate fragments shed from giant marrow cells called megakaryocytes. They are not immature red cells.

test.q: How long does a typical red blood cell survive in circulation?
test.explain: Red cells live about 120 days before the spleen and liver remove them. About 10 days is closer to platelet survival.

test.q: Serum differs from plasma because serum lacks:
test.explain: Serum is the fluid left after blood clots, so fibrinogen and other clotting factors have been used up. Albumin, glucose and sodium remain.

test.q: Albumin's main job in plasma is:
test.explain: Albumin generates most of the plasma oncotic pressure, which holds fluid inside capillaries. Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin inside red cells.

test.q: Which statement defines the hematocrit?
choices: Share of blood volume taken by red cells
Count of white cells per microliter
Ratio of plasma proteins to plasma water
Grams of hemoglobin per liter of blood
test.explain: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume occupied by red cells. Hemoglobin concentration is a separate measurement.

test.q: Mature red cells lack a nucleus and mitochondria. One key advantage is that:
choices: They can repair damage to their own proteins
They do not consume the oxygen they carry
They make new hemoglobin throughout life
They can divide quickly when oxygen is low
test.explain: Without mitochondria, red cells make ATP by anaerobic glycolysis and leave their oxygen cargo for the tissues. Lacking a nucleus, they cannot divide or make new proteins.

test.q: What is the name of the liquid left over after blood has been allowed to clot?
test.explain: Serum is plasma minus fibrinogen and the consumed clotting factors.

test.q: Platelets are shed from giant bone marrow cells called ___.
test.explain: Megakaryocytes release platelets as small anucleate fragments.

test.q: What is the oxygen-carrying protein packed inside red blood cells?
test.explain: Hemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.

kidTest.q: What color is plasma, the liquid part of blood?
kidTest.explain: Plasma is a yellow liquid. The red color of blood comes from red blood cells.

kidTest.q: Which cells carry oxygen around your body?
kidTest.explain: Red blood cells are the delivery trucks for oxygen.

kidTest.q: What do platelets do when you get a cut?
kidTest.explain: Platelets rush to the cut and stick together to plug it.

kidTest.q: Where are blood cells made?
kidTest.explain: Blood cells are made in the soft marrow inside your bones.

kidTest.q: Tiny pieces in blood that make a plug at a cut: p _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Platelets are tiny pieces that help stop bleeding.

advancedTest.q: Ten minutes after a sudden large hemorrhage, before any IV fluids, the patient's hematocrit is most likely to:
choices: Stay near baseline until plasma volume is restored
Fall at once because red cells are lost faster than plasma
Rise because stored red cells enter the bloodstream
Fall at once because the marrow halts red cell output
advancedTest.explain: Whole blood is lost in proportion, so the ratio of cells to plasma hardly changes at first. Hematocrit falls only as interstitial fluid or IV fluids refill the plasma.

advancedTest.q: A well patient with no bleeding has an analyzer platelet count far below normal from an EDTA tube, and the smear shows aggregates. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Antibodies aggregate platelets after the draw
Immune destruction of platelets in the spleen
Megakaryocytes fail to release new platelets
Platelets diluted by expanded plasma volume
advancedTest.explain: This is EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia: platelets stick together in the tube and are not counted. Repeating the count in citrate confirms it, whereas true destruction would not produce aggregates on the smear.

advancedTest.q: Why does blood flow through small arterioles with lower apparent viscosity than bulk blood measured in a wide tube?
choices: Plasma proteins are filtered out as the vessels narrow
Red cells stiffen so they can slide more easily past each other
Cells gather centrally, leaving a plasma layer at the wall
Platelets coat the vessel wall and so lower its friction
advancedTest.explain: In the Fåhræus–Lindqvist effect, deformable red cells migrate to the vessel axis and leave a low-viscosity cell-free layer at the wall. Stiffer red cells would raise viscosity, not lower it.

advancedTest.q: A patient with marked thrombocytosis has high serum potassium, but a heparinized plasma sample is normal and the ECG shows no changes. Best explanation?
choices: Platelets release potassium as the sample clots
Plasma proteins hide potassium from the analyzer
Insulin is shifting potassium out of body cells
The kidneys are failing to excrete enough potassium
advancedTest.explain: During in vitro clotting, platelets release intracellular potassium into serum, producing pseudohyperkalemia. A true increase in body potassium would raise the plasma level too and risk ECG changes.

lessons.title: Hematopoietic Stem Cells & the Bone Marrow Niche

levels.kid:
Your blood is full of tiny cells, and they wear out. A red blood cell lasts only about four months. So your body needs a factory that never stops.

That factory is the **bone marrow**, the soft, spongy stuff inside your bones. Hidden in the marrow are special cells called **stem cells**. A blood stem cell is like a magic seed. It can copy itself to make more seeds. It can also grow into any kind of blood cell: red cells, white cells or platelets.

Stem cells live in a cozy home called a **niche**. Helper cells in the niche send messages that say "rest" or "get to work." Most of the time, stem cells rest quietly. Resting keeps them safe and healthy, so they can keep making blood for your whole life.
levels.hs:
**Hematopoiesis** is the making of blood cells. Your body produces hundreds of billions of new blood cells every day to replace the ones that wear out.

All of them trace back to **hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs)**, rare cells in the **bone marrow**. HSCs have two defining properties:
- **Self-renewal**: when they divide, they can make new stem cells, so the supply doesn't run out.
- **Multipotency**: they can produce every type of blood cell, including red cells, platelets and all the white cells.

In adults, active **red marrow** is found mainly in the pelvis, sternum, vertebrae, ribs and skull. The shafts of the long bones fill with fatty **yellow marrow**. Before birth, blood is made first in the yolk sac, then mainly in the fetal liver, and finally in the marrow.

HSCs don't act alone. They live in a **niche**, a local support environment made of blood vessels, stromal (support) cells, bone cells and nerves. The niche sends signals that tell HSCs when to rest, divide or specialize. Most HSCs spend most of their time resting, a state called **quiescence**, which protects them from DNA damage and from being used up.

Real example: in a **bone marrow transplant**, donor HSCs are infused into a vein. They travel to the patient's marrow niches and rebuild the entire blood system. Doctors use this treatment for leukemia and other blood diseases.
levels.college:
**The hierarchy.** Hematopoiesis is organized as a branching tree with **long-term HSCs (LT-HSCs)** at the top. Below them sit short-term HSCs and **multipotent progenitors (MPPs)**, which divide more but self-renew less. These give rise to lineage-committed progenitors:
- **Common myeloid progenitor (CMP)**: splits into megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors (platelets, red cells) and granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (neutrophils, monocytes).
- **Common lymphoid progenitor (CLP)**: gives rise to T cells, B cells and NK cells.

At each step, cells gain specialized function and lose self-renewal. True HSCs are rare, on the order of 1 in 10,000 to 100,000 marrow cells.

**Identifying HSCs.** Human HSCs are enriched among cells expressing the surface marker **CD34** and lacking CD38. CD34+ cell counts are used to measure and collect stem cell grafts. Mouse HSCs are classically Lin− Sca-1+ c-Kit+ (LSK) cells, refined further by the SLAM code CD150+ CD48−.

**Where they come from.** Primitive red cells first appear in the yolk sac. Definitive HSCs emerge from specialized endothelium in the **aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM)** region through an endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition, expand in the fetal liver, and settle in the marrow around birth.

**The niche.** Key niche signals:
- **CXCL12** (also called SDF-1), a chemokine made by perivascular stromal cells, binds **CXCR4** on HSCs and anchors them in the marrow.
- **Stem cell factor (SCF)** binds the receptor **c-Kit** on HSCs and supports their survival and maintenance.
- Low oxygen, signals from megakaryocytes, and sympathetic nerves help regulate quiescence and release.

**Mobilization.** Disrupting retention moves HSCs into the circulating blood, where they can be collected by apheresis. G-CSF does this indirectly, and **plerixafor** blocks CXCR4, cutting the CXCL12 anchor. Most transplant grafts today are collected this way rather than from a marrow harvest.
levels.phd:
**Founding experiments.** In 1961 Till and McCulloch injected marrow into irradiated mice and saw macroscopic **spleen colonies (CFU-S)**, each arising from a single cell. Later marker studies showed that colonies contained multiple lineages and self-renewing cells. Definitive single-cell proof came from Osawa et al. (1996), who reconstituted a mouse's entire hematopoietic system with one CD34−/low c-Kit+ Sca-1+ Lin− cell. In humans, Notta et al. (2011) added CD49f, enriching single cells capable of long-term engraftment in immunodeficient mice (CD34+ CD38− CD45RA− CD90+ CD49f+).

**The niche concept.** Schofield proposed the niche in 1978. Early work emphasized the **endosteal** (bone-lining) niche after osteoblast expansion was linked to HSC increases (Calvi; Zhang, 2003). Conditional deletion studies reshaped this view: Ding and Morrison (2012, 2013) showed that deleting **SCF** from endothelial cells and **leptin receptor-positive (LepR+) perivascular stromal cells** depleted HSCs, whereas deletion from osteoblasts did not. CXCL12 from the same perivascular population (the CXCL12-abundant reticular, or **CAR, cells** described by Nagasawa) also maintains HSCs. Deep imaging by Acar et al. (2015) placed most HSCs next to sinusoids, contesting a model of quiescent HSCs near arterioles (Kunisaki 2013). Megakaryocytes enforce quiescence via CXCL4 and TGF-β1, and sympathetic signals drive circadian HSC egress (Méndez-Ferrer 2008).

**Quiescence and metabolism.** The most dormant HSCs divide roughly every five months in mice (label retention, Wilson 2008). They favor glycolysis, keep reactive oxygen species low, depend on HIF-1α, and tightly limit protein synthesis. Interferons and infection can force exit from dormancy.

**Rethinking the tree.** Single-cell transcriptomics (Velten 2017) and functional studies (Notta 2016) suggest commitment is a continuum rather than neat stepwise bifurcations, and some HSCs are platelet-biased (vWF+ in mice). Inducible lineage tracing and barcoding in unperturbed mice (Sun 2014; Busch 2015) indicated that MPPs and long-lived progenitors carry much of the daily output, while LT-HSCs feed in slowly. Transplantation, the classic gold standard, therefore measures potential under stress, not native behavior.
levels.expert:
**Transplantation in practice.** E. Donnall Thomas pioneered marrow transplantation (Nobel Prize 1990). Grafts now come from mobilized peripheral blood (most common in adults), marrow harvest, or umbilical cord blood. Graft adequacy is judged by **CD34+ cell count**, and homing back to empty niches depends on CXCR4–CXCL12 and adhesion molecules such as VLA-4. Poor mobilizers, for example after lenalidomide, fludarabine or heavy prior chemotherapy, often need plerixafor. Cord blood tolerates more HLA mismatch but contains far fewer CD34+ cells, so neutrophil engraftment is slow. **Omidubicel** (approved 2023), a nicotinamide-expanded cord product, shortens neutrophil recovery; small molecules such as UM171 are also in trials for ex vivo expansion.

**Gene therapy rides on niche biology.** **Exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy)**, approved in late 2023 for sickle cell disease and early 2024 for transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia, uses CRISPR–Cas9 to disrupt the erythroid BCL11A enhancer in the patient's own CD34+ cells, reactivating fetal hemoglobin. Edited cells need vacated niches, so patients still receive myeloablative busulfan, with infertility and organ toxicity risks. Antibody-based conditioning targeting CD117 (c-Kit) or CD45 aims to clear niches without chemotherapy.

**Clonal hematopoiesis.** Aging HSCs accumulate mutations. A driver-mutant clone at a variant allele fraction of at least 2%, without cytopenias or a blood cancer, is **CHIP** (clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential). Most common in DNMT3A, TET2 and ASXL1, it rises steeply after age 70, carries roughly 0.5–1% per year risk of hematologic cancer, and roughly doubles coronary disease risk, partly via inflammatory macrophages (Jaiswal 2014, 2017). It can confound tumor sequencing and complicates selecting older related donors.

**Aging niche.** Aged HSCs expand in number but lose function and skew toward myeloid and platelet output, while the niche becomes inflamed and adipocyte-rich.

**Neuro link.** Skull marrow connects to the dura through microscopic vascular channels (Herisson 2018), supplying meningeal myeloid cells and B cells during stroke and infection (Cugurra 2021), a reminder that the cranium is an immune organ.

**Open questions:** the true human niche architecture, safe in vivo HSC editing, and expansion without loss of stemness.

keyPoints: HSCs are defined by self-renewal plus multipotency (they can make every blood cell type)
Adult red marrow sits mainly in the pelvis, sternum, vertebrae, ribs and skull
Development: yolk sac, then AGM-derived HSCs in fetal liver, then bone marrow
The niche (perivascular LepR+ cells, endothelium) supplies CXCL12 and SCF to keep HSCs
Most HSCs are quiescent, protecting them from DNA damage and exhaustion
Blocking CXCR4 (plerixafor) or giving G-CSF mobilizes HSCs for CD34+ grafts

test.q: Which two properties define a hematopoietic stem cell?
test.explain: HSCs can make more of themselves (self-renewal) and can produce every blood cell type (multipotency). Rapid division is more typical of progenitors, not resting HSCs.

test.q: In adults, where is most active red marrow found?
choices: Shafts of the long limb bones
test.explain: Adult red marrow is concentrated in the axial skeleton. The shafts of long bones fill with fatty yellow marrow.

test.q: In hematology, the bone marrow 'niche' is best described as:
choices: The local support environment for stem cells
A type of white blood cell in the marrow
A protein carrying oxygen in red cells
The fatty yellow tissue inside long bones
test.explain: The niche is the microenvironment of vessels, stromal cells, bone cells and nerves that signals HSCs to rest, divide or specialize.

test.q: Which chemokine, made by perivascular stromal cells, binds CXCR4 and anchors HSCs in the marrow?
test.explain: CXCL12 (SDF-1) binds CXCR4 on HSCs and retains them in the marrow. Erythropoietin drives red cell production, not retention.

test.q: Which drug mobilizes HSCs into the circulation by blocking CXCR4?
test.explain: Plerixafor blocks CXCR4, cutting the CXCL12 anchor so HSCs enter the blood for collection. Heparin and warfarin are anticoagulants.

test.q: Most HSCs spend their time in a resting state called quiescence. Why is this useful?
choices: It shields them from DNA damage
It helps them leave the marrow
It lets them carry more oxygen
It speeds up red cell production
test.explain: Resting protects HSCs from DNA damage and from being used up, preserving the stem cell pool for life.

test.q: In what order do sites of blood formation appear during development?
choices: Liver, then yolk sac, then spleen
Marrow, then liver, then yolk sac
Yolk sac, then liver, then marrow
test.explain: Primitive blood forms in the yolk sac; definitive HSCs from the AGM region expand in the fetal liver and then settle in the marrow around birth.

test.q: Which surface marker is used to measure and collect human stem cell grafts?
test.explain: Human HSCs are enriched among CD34+ CD38− cells, and CD34+ counts judge graft adequacy. CD4, CD3 and CD19 mark mature T or B cells.

test.q: Till and McCulloch's 1961 experiments showed that single marrow cells could form colonies in which organ of irradiated mice?
test.explain: They observed spleen colonies (CFU-S), each from one cell, the first experimental evidence for blood-forming stem cells.

test.q: Which progenitor gives rise to T cells, B cells and NK cells?
test.explain: The common lymphoid progenitor (CLP) produces lymphocytes, while the common myeloid progenitor produces red cells, platelets, granulocytes and monocytes.

test.q: The niche signal that binds the c-Kit receptor on HSCs is called ___ (abbreviated SCF).
test.explain: Stem cell factor, made by endothelial and LepR+ perivascular cells, binds c-Kit and maintains HSCs.

test.q: The process of making new blood cells is called ___.
test.explain: Hematopoiesis produces hundreds of billions of blood cells every day, all tracing back to HSCs.

kidTest.q: Where does your body make new blood cells?
kidTest.explain: Blood cells are made in the soft marrow inside your bones.

kidTest.q: What can a blood stem cell do?
choices: Copy itself and make new cells
Break down the food you eat
kidTest.explain: A stem cell is like a magic seed: it copies itself and grows into all kinds of blood cells.

kidTest.q: The niche where stem cells live is like:
choices: A big wall that blocks cells
kidTest.explain: The niche is a cozy home where helper cells send messages to the stem cells.

kidTest.q: What do blood stem cells do most of the time?
kidTest.explain: Stem cells rest most of the time, which keeps them safe and healthy.

kidTest.q: The soft, spongy stuff inside your bones is called m _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Bone marrow is the blood factory inside your bones.

advancedTest.q: Deleting SCF from endothelial and LepR+ perivascular cells depletes HSCs, but deleting it from osteoblasts does not. The best conclusion is:
choices: SCF is dispensable for HSC maintenance in vivo
HSCs make enough SCF to sustain themselves
Osteoblasts are the main source of SCF for HSCs
HSCs rely mainly on perivascular cells for SCF
advancedTest.explain: Ding and Morrison's deletions show the functionally important SCF comes from perivascular and endothelial cells, shifting emphasis away from the endosteal osteoblast niche.

advancedTest.q: Lineage tracing in unperturbed mice suggests steady-state blood output relies heavily on MPPs and long-lived progenitors. What does this imply about classic transplantation assays?
choices: They show HSCs are inactive under stress
They may overstate native HSC output
They measure native output without bias
They prove progenitors outlive true HSCs
advancedTest.explain: Transplantation measures what HSCs can do under stress, not what they normally do. Native tracing shows LT-HSCs feed in slowly while progenitors carry much daily output.

advancedTest.q: A 70-year-old with normal blood counts has a DNMT3A mutation at 8% variant allele fraction in blood. The best interpretation is:
choices: CHIP with higher heart and blood cancer risk
An inherited germline variant from a parent
A sequencing artifact likely to vanish
advancedTest.explain: A driver mutation at 2% or more without cytopenias or cancer defines CHIP, which raises cardiovascular and hematologic cancer risk. A germline variant would sit near 50%, and normal counts argue against leukemia.

advancedTest.q: Unmanipulated cord blood grafts engraft more slowly than mobilized peripheral blood grafts mainly because:
choices: Cord blood needs closer HLA matching
Cord blood cells lack CXCR4 receptors
They contain fewer total CD34+ cells
advancedTest.explain: Cell dose limits cord blood engraftment, which is why expansion products like omidubicel help. Cord blood actually tolerates more HLA mismatch, not less.

lessons.title: Growth Factors That Steer Cell Fate: EPO, TPO & CSFs

levels.kid:
Your bone marrow is like a busy factory making blood cells all day. But how does it know how many of each kind to make? Special messenger chemicals called **growth factors** travel through your blood and tell the factory what to build.

**EPO** (made by your kidneys) tells the marrow to make more red blood cells when your body needs more oxygen, like after losing blood or living high in the mountains. **TPO** (made mostly by your liver) tells the marrow to make platelets, the tiny pieces that plug up cuts. Other messengers called **CSFs** tell the marrow to make more white blood cells to fight germs.

Doctors can even give these messengers as medicines to help sick people make more of the blood cells they're missing.
levels.hs:
Bone marrow produces billions of new blood cells every day, and it adjusts production based on the body's needs using chemical messengers called **hematopoietic growth factors**. These are proteins that bind receptors on stem and progenitor cells, pushing them to divide and mature into specific cell types.

**Erythropoietin (EPO)** is made mainly by the kidneys in response to low oxygen levels (hypoxia). It signals the marrow to produce more red blood cells. People with kidney failure often become anemic because damaged kidneys cannot make enough EPO; doctors can treat this with synthetic EPO injections.

**Thrombopoietin (TPO)** is produced mainly by the liver and stimulates megakaryocytes, the large marrow cells that break apart to release platelets. TPO levels rise when platelet counts are low.

**Colony-stimulating factors (CSFs)**, such as G-CSF and GM-CSF, stimulate production of white blood cells, especially neutrophils, which fight bacterial infections. G-CSF is given to cancer patients whose white counts drop dangerously low after chemotherapy, helping them recover faster and avoid serious infections.

Together these growth factors form feedback loops: when a cell type runs low, the body senses it and ramps up the matching growth factor to restore balance.
levels.college:
Hematopoiesis is tightly regulated by a network of glycoprotein growth factors that act on hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) through specific cell-surface receptors, triggering intracellular signaling cascades (commonly JAK-STAT pathways) that promote proliferation, survival, and lineage-specific differentiation.

- **Erythropoietin (EPO)**: produced by renal peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in response to tissue hypoxia, sensed via the transcription factor hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). EPO binds the EPO receptor on erythroid progenitors (burst-forming unit-erythroid, BFU-E, and colony-forming unit-erythroid, CFU-E), activating JAK2-STAT5 signaling to promote their survival and maturation into reticulocytes. Chronic kidney disease reduces EPO output, causing anemia of renal disease; recombinant EPO (epoetin) restores red cell production but carries thrombotic risk if hemoglobin is raised too aggressively.

- **Thrombopoietin (TPO)**: synthesized constitutively by hepatocytes, and its circulating level is inversely related to platelet and megakaryocyte mass, which absorb and clear TPO via the c-Mpl receptor. TPO drives megakaryocyte proliferation, polyploidization (endomitosis), and platelet shedding. TPO receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag) are used clinically for chronic immune thrombocytopenia.

- **Colony-stimulating factors (CSFs)**: G-CSF stimulates neutrophil precursors specifically; GM-CSF acts more broadly on granulocyte and monocyte lineages; M-CSF supports monocyte/macrophage development. These are produced locally by marrow stromal cells, endothelium, and activated immune cells, often in response to infection or inflammation (via cytokines like IL-1 and TNF-alpha). Recombinant G-CSF (filgrastim) shortens neutropenia after chemotherapy or stem cell transplant.

These factors act combinatorially with early-acting cytokines like IL-3 and stem cell factor (SCF/KIT ligand), which support multipotent progenitors before lineage-specific factors commit cells to a single fate.
levels.phd:
Hematopoietic growth factors operate within a hierarchical signaling architecture: early, broadly acting cytokines (SCF/KIT ligand, IL-3, FLT3 ligand) sustain multipotent progenitor survival and proliferation, while late-acting, lineage-restricted factors (EPO, TPO, G-CSF, GM-CSF, M-CSF) drive terminal commitment and maturation. Most of these factors signal through type I cytokine receptors lacking intrinsic kinase activity, instead associating constitutively with Janus kinases (JAK2 for EPOR and MPL, JAK2/JAK1 for GM-CSF receptor) that trans-phosphorylate upon receptor dimerization, activating STAT5, PI3K-AKT, and RAS-MAPK pathways.

EPO regulation exemplifies an elegant oxygen-sensing circuit: under normoxia, prolyl hydroxylase domain enzymes (PHDs) hydroxylate HIF-alpha, targeting it for VHL-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Hypoxia inhibits PHDs, stabilizing HIF-2alpha in renal interstitial fibroblasts, which transactivates the EPO gene. This pathway is now druggable: HIF-PHD inhibitors (roxadustat, daprodustat) stimulate endogenous EPO production and are used for anemia of chronic kidney disease, offering an oral alternative to injectable recombinant EPO, though cardiovascular and thrombotic safety remain under scrutiny (controversy highlighted in trials like PRO2TECT and OLYMPUS).

TPO biology reveals a passive clearance model of homeostasis: free hepatic TPO production is largely constitutive, and circulating TPO levels are set by MPL-mediated uptake and degradation by platelets and megakaryocytes, so thrombocytopenia (fewer sinks) raises free TPO, while thrombocytosis lowers it—essentially a clearance-based rheostat rather than classical feedback transcriptional control.

Clinically, excessive or chronic growth factor receptor signaling underlies several neoplasms: constitutively active JAK2 V617F mutation drives polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis by mimicking ligand-independent EPOR/MPL signaling—directly implicating these growth factor pathways in myeloproliferative disease pathogenesis.
levels.expert:
Clinically, manipulation of hematopoietic growth factor pathways illustrates both their power and their pitfalls. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) dramatically improved quality of life for dialysis and chemotherapy-induced anemia patients, but landmark trials (CHOIR, TREAT) showed that targeting higher hemoglobin targets with ESAs increased cardiovascular events and stroke risk without mortality benefit, leading to more conservative hemoglobin targets in current guidelines. The mechanism is thought to involve off-target EPOR signaling on vascular endothelium and platelets, promoting a prothrombotic state independent of red cell mass.

HIF-PHD inhibitors represent a genuinely novel drug class (first approved in several countries for renal anemia), acting by stabilizing endogenous HIF rather than supplying exogenous hormone; they also modestly raise hepcidin-suppressing effects, improving iron availability, but long-term oncologic safety is still debated since HIF pathways also support tumor angiogenesis.

TPO receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag) transformed management of chronic immune thrombocytopenia, allowing sustained platelet responses without ongoing immunosuppression; eltrombopag additionally chelates intracellular iron pools in a way that paradoxically supports trilineage hematopoiesis in aplastic anemia, now used alongside immunosuppressive therapy for patients ineligible for stem cell transplant.

G-CSF use carries nuanced risks: in healthy stem cell donors it is generally safe, but rare reports of splenic rupture and theoretical concern for accelerating latent myeloid clones warrant caution. In myelodysplastic syndromes, G-CSF must be used carefully since some clones show abnormal proliferative responses.

An open question is whether growth factor receptor agonism can be fine-tuned to avoid activating prothrombotic or malignant-prone signaling arms (e.g., biased agonists favoring STAT5 over other branches), an active area of protein engineering. Discovery of JAK2 V617F also spurred JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib) as targeted therapy for myeloproliferative neoplasms, directly translating basic growth-factor signaling biology into clinical oncology.

keyPoints: Hematopoietic growth factors are signaling proteins that direct stem/progenitor cells toward specific blood cell lineages
EPO, made by the kidney in response to hypoxia via the HIF pathway, stimulates red blood cell production
TPO, made mainly by the liver, stimulates megakaryocytes to produce platelets and is regulated by clearance via platelet MPL receptors
CSFs (G-CSF, GM-CSF, M-CSF) stimulate production of white blood cells, especially neutrophils
Most growth factor receptors signal through JAK-STAT pathways
Growth factors are used clinically (recombinant EPO, TPO agonists, G-CSF) and their dysregulation (e.g. JAK2 mutation) can cause disease

test.q: Which organ primarily produces erythropoietin (EPO)?
test.explain: EPO is produced mainly by renal interstitial fibroblasts in response to hypoxia; the liver makes a smaller amount.

test.q: What triggers increased EPO production?
test.explain: EPO production rises when tissue oxygen is low, signaled through stabilization of HIF.

test.q: Thrombopoietin (TPO) mainly stimulates production of:
test.explain: TPO acts on megakaryocytes, driving platelet production.

test.q: Which organ is the main constitutive source of TPO?
test.explain: Hepatocytes continuously produce TPO; its free level depends on clearance by platelets/megakaryocytes.

test.q: G-CSF is primarily used clinically to boost:
choices: Red blood cells after blood loss
test.explain: G-CSF stimulates neutrophil production and is given to patients with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.

test.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease often develops anemia because:
choices: Damaged kidneys make too little EPO
Platelets are destroying red blood cells
Liver stops making enough TPO hormone
G-CSF levels rise far too high
test.explain: Kidney damage reduces EPO production, which is needed to stimulate red cell production.

test.q: Which signaling pathway is commonly activated by EPO and TPO receptors?
test.explain: EPO and TPO receptors lack intrinsic kinase activity but associate with JAK kinases that activate STAT signaling.

test.q: GM-CSF differs from G-CSF in that GM-CSF:
choices: Acts across granulocyte and monocyte lineages
Acts mainly on red cell precursors
Is produced mainly by the kidney
test.explain: GM-CSF has a broader effect across granulocyte and monocyte development, while G-CSF is more neutrophil-specific.

test.q: TPO receptor agonists like romiplostim are used to treat:
test.explain: These drugs stimulate platelet production and help patients with chronic immune thrombocytopenia maintain safe platelet counts.

test.q: What transcription factor is stabilized under low oxygen and drives EPO gene expression?
test.explain: Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) accumulates under low oxygen and activates transcription of the EPO gene.

test.q: Megakaryocytes break apart to release ___, which are needed to plug small blood vessel injuries.
test.explain: Platelets bud off from megakaryocytes under TPO stimulation.

test.q: What is the receptor for thrombopoietin called?
test.explain: TPO binds the MPL receptor on megakaryocytes and platelets, which also clears TPO from circulation.

kidTest.q: What does EPO tell the bone marrow to make more of?
kidTest.explain: EPO signals the marrow to produce more red blood cells, especially when oxygen is low.

kidTest.q: Which organ mostly makes EPO?
kidTest.explain: The kidneys sense low oxygen and release EPO.

kidTest.q: What does TPO help the body make?
kidTest.explain: TPO tells the marrow to make platelets, which help stop bleeding.

kidTest.q: What do CSFs help the marrow make more of?
kidTest.explain: CSFs (colony-stimulating factors) boost white blood cell production to fight germs.

kidTest.q: What word (starts with g) describes chemicals that tell marrow cells how to grow? g _ _ _ _ _ factors
kidTest.explain: These are called growth factors because they signal bone marrow cells to grow and mature into specific blood cells. Examples include EPO for red cells, TPO for platelets, and CSFs for white cells.

advancedTest.q: Why is TPO regulation described as a 'clearance-based rheostat' rather than classical feedback transcription?
choices: TPO is degraded by the kidney based on oxygen levels
Free TPO rises when fewer platelets absorb it via MPL
TPO production largely halts when platelet counts are normal
TPO gene transcription rises directly when platelet counts drop
advancedTest.explain: Hepatic TPO production is largely constant; circulating levels depend on how much is cleared by MPL receptors on platelets and megakaryocytes, so fewer platelets mean more free TPO.

advancedTest.q: HIF-PHD inhibitors treat anemia by:
choices: Inhibiting JAK2 signaling at the EPO receptor
Blocking HIF degradation to raise EPO transcription
advancedTest.explain: These drugs inhibit prolyl hydroxylases, preventing HIF degradation, so HIF accumulates and drives endogenous EPO gene expression.

advancedTest.q: The JAK2 V617F mutation causes myeloproliferative neoplasms by:
choices: Increasing clearance of TPO by platelets
Disrupting EPOR and MPL signaling broadly
advancedTest.explain: The mutation causes JAK2 to signal continuously without needing EPO or TPO binding, driving excess cell production.

advancedTest.q: A key safety concern that emerged from trials of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents targeting higher hemoglobin levels was:
choices: Worsened kidney function unrelated to clotting
advancedTest.explain: Trials like CHOIR and TREAT found higher hemoglobin targets with ESAs raised cardiovascular and stroke risk, likely via off-target EPOR signaling on endothelium and platelets.

lessons.title: Plasma Proteins: Albumin, Globulins & Fibrinogen

levels.kid:
Blood is more than red cells. More than half of it is a pale yellow liquid called **plasma**. Plasma is mostly water, but it is like a soup with tiny helpers floating in it. These helpers are **proteins**, and your liver is the factory that makes most of them.

- **Albumin** is like a sponge. It holds water inside your blood vessels so it does not leak out and make you puffy.
- **Globulins** are a team. Some are delivery trucks that carry things around. Some are antibodies that fight germs.
- **Fibrinogen** is a thread-maker. When you get a cut, it turns into sticky threads. The threads make a net that plugs the leak.

Together, these proteins keep your blood working just right!
levels.hs:
**Plasma** is the liquid part of blood, about 55% of its volume. It is roughly 92% water. Dissolved in it are salts, sugar, hormones and about 60-80 grams of protein per liter. There are three main groups of **plasma proteins**:

- **Albumin** is the most abundant, a little over half of all plasma protein. It is made by the liver. Because it is too big to slip easily through capillary walls, it pulls water back into the blood. This pull is called **oncotic pressure**. Albumin also carries things that do not dissolve well in water, like fatty acids, bilirubin, calcium and many medicines.
- **Globulins** are a mixed group. Some carry iron or copper; others, the **immunoglobulins**, are antibodies that fight infection.
- **Fibrinogen** is a clotting protein. When a vessel is injured, the enzyme **thrombin** cuts fibrinogen into **fibrin**, which forms the threads of a clot.

If you let blood clot in a tube, the liquid left over is called **serum**. Serum is plasma without fibrinogen and the other clotting factors that were used up.

Real example: in **nephrotic syndrome**, damaged kidneys leak albumin into the urine. Albumin levels drop, oncotic pressure falls, and fluid seeps into tissues, causing swelling (**edema**) around the eyes and ankles.
levels.college:
Plasma contains roughly 60-80 g/L of protein. Most of it, except the immunoglobulins, is synthesized by **hepatocytes** in the liver.

**Albumin** (about 35-50 g/L) has several jobs:
- Generates roughly 80% of plasma **colloid oncotic pressure**, opposing hydrostatic pressure in Starling's balance of capillary fluid exchange.
- Acts as a carrier for unconjugated bilirubin, free fatty acids, thyroid hormone, about 40% of calcium, and many drugs. Only the **unbound (free) fraction** of a drug is active, so low albumin can raise free drug levels.
- Contributes to acid-base buffering and antioxidant capacity.

**Globulins** are separated by **serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP)** into bands:
- **Alpha-1**: alpha-1-antitrypsin, a protease inhibitor.
- **Alpha-2**: haptoglobin (binds free hemoglobin), ceruloplasmin (copper), alpha-2-macroglobulin.
- **Beta**: transferrin (iron transport), complement C3, LDL.
- **Gamma**: immunoglobulins, made by **plasma cells** (differentiated B cells).

A broad gamma increase (**polyclonal**) suggests chronic inflammation or liver disease. A narrow spike (**M-protein**) suggests a single plasma cell clone, as in MGUS or multiple myeloma.

**Fibrinogen** (about 2-4 g/L) is the substrate of coagulation. Thrombin cleaves small fibrinopeptides from it, exposing binding sites so fibrin monomers polymerize into strands. **Factor XIIIa** then cross-links the strands, stabilizing the clot. Fibrinogen also bridges activated platelets by binding their **GPIIb/IIIa** receptors.

**Acute phase response.** During inflammation, cytokines (especially IL-6) shift liver output:
- Up: fibrinogen, C-reactive protein, haptoglobin, ferritin.
- Down (negative acute phase reactants): albumin, transferrin.

This is why low albumin in hospitalized patients often reflects inflammation rather than poor nutrition.
levels.phd:
**Albumin** is a 585-residue, roughly 66.5 kDa non-glycosylated protein folded into three homologous helical domains. It has no classic hormone-like receptor function; its biology is binding and volume. Drug binding concentrates at **Sudlow site I** (subdomain IIA; warfarin, azapropazone) and **Sudlow site II** (IIIA; benzodiazepines, ibuprofen), plus multiple fatty-acid sites whose occupancy allosterically alters drug affinity. A single free thiol, **Cys34**, makes albumin the dominant plasma thiol and a scavenger of reactive species. Albumin's ~3-week half-life comes from pH-dependent rescue by the neonatal Fc receptor (**FcRn**) in endothelial cells, which binds albumin and IgG at distinct sites in acidic endosomes and returns them to the surface instead of lysosomes. Synthesis is regulated by colloid osmotic pressure in the hepatic interstitium and suppressed by IL-6 and TNF.

The oncotic story has a nuance. Patients with congenital **analbuminemia** (ALB gene mutations) have only mild edema, partly because globulins rise and interstitial protein falls, preserving the transcapillary oncotic gradient. The **revised Starling principle** (Levick and Michel) adds that the relevant oncotic gradient is across the endothelial **glycocalyx**, and that sustained reabsorption in most capillaries is minimal; lymph returns most filtrate.

**Fibrinogen** (~340 kDa) is a dimer of three chains, (Aα, Bβ, γ)2, encoded by **FGA, FGB and FGG** on chromosome 4. Thrombin releases **fibrinopeptide A** first, exposing knob A that docks into hole a in the γ-chain of a neighbor, driving half-staggered protofibril assembly; fibrinopeptide B release promotes lateral aggregation. Factor XIIIa forms γ-γ and α-chain isopeptide cross-links, increasing stiffness and resistance to plasmin. Fibrinogen is a major IL-6/STAT3-driven acute phase reactant.

Fibrinogen also explains the **erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)**: as a large asymmetric molecule it reduces the negative surface repulsion (zeta potential) between red cells, promoting **rouleaux** that settle faster. Albumin opposes this, so the ESR rises when fibrinogen and globulins rise and albumin falls.

Inherited disorders include afibrinogenemia, hypofibrinogenemia and **dysfibrinogenemia**, the last paradoxically linked to bleeding, thrombosis or both depending on the variant.
levels.expert:
Clinically, plasma proteins are most useful as signals and most dangerous when misread.

**Albumin pitfalls**
- Hypoalbuminemia in inpatients mainly reflects inflammation, capillary leak, dilution and losses, not intake. Guidelines no longer use it as a malnutrition marker.
- Total levels of highly bound drugs mislead. With phenytoin in hypoalbuminemia or uremia, a total level in the usual range can hide a toxic free level; measure free drug.
- Albumin-adjusted calcium formulas perform poorly in critical illness; measure ionized calcium.

**Albumin as therapy.** The **SAFE** trial (2004) found 4% albumin and saline equivalent for ICU resuscitation, but the **SAFE-TBI** analysis showed higher mortality with albumin in traumatic brain injury, linked to raised intracranial pressure, possibly because that solution is mildly hypotonic. That matters for neurosurgical patients. **ALBIOS** (2014) showed no overall survival benefit in severe sepsis. In cirrhosis, albumin has established roles with large-volume paracentesis and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, but **ATTIRE** (2021) found targeted albumin replacement in hospitalized decompensated cirrhosis gave no benefit and more pulmonary edema.

**Fibrinogen in hemorrhage.** It is the first factor to fall to critical levels in major bleeding from consumption, loss and dilution. The **Clauss assay** can be distorted by direct thrombin inhibitors and high fibrin degradation products; viscoelastic tests (ROTEM FIBTEM, TEG functional fibrinogen) give faster, functional estimates. **FIBRES** (2019) found fibrinogen concentrate noninferior to cryoprecipitate in cardiac surgery, while **CRYOSTAT-2** (2023) found routine early cryoprecipitate in trauma did not reduce mortality.

**Pharmacology frontiers**
- **Albumin hitchhiking**: semaglutide's fatty-acid side chain binds albumin, stretching its half-life to about a week; nab-paclitaxel uses albumin as a solvent-free carrier.
- **FcRn blockade** (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab, nipocalimab) lowers IgG to treat myasthenia gravis and other antibody diseases. Some agents in the class, notably batoclimab, also reduced albumin and raised LDL, a reminder that FcRn guards both proteins.

Open questions: whether glycocalyx-protective strategies outperform albumin, and whether albumin's binding and antioxidant functions, not just its level, should guide therapy.

keyPoints: Plasma holds about 60-80 g/L of protein, mostly made by the liver
Albumin is the most abundant and provides most oncotic pressure
Albumin carries bilirubin, fatty acids, calcium and many drugs; only free drug is active
Globulins split into alpha, beta and gamma bands; gamma globulins are antibodies from plasma cells
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, which factor XIIIa cross-links into a stable clot
In inflammation fibrinogen and CRP rise while albumin and transferrin fall

test.q: Which protein makes up the largest share of total plasma protein?
test.explain: Albumin is a little over half of all plasma protein. Fibrinogen, despite its importance in clotting, is only a few percent.

test.q: Albumin keeps fluid inside blood vessels mainly by generating:
test.explain: Albumin is too large to cross capillary walls easily, so it pulls water back into the blood (oncotic pressure). Hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out.

test.q: Serum differs from plasma because serum lacks:
test.explain: Serum is the liquid left after blood clots, so fibrinogen and other clotting factors have been used up. Albumin and antibodies remain.

test.q: Gamma globulins (immunoglobulins) are mainly produced by which cells?
test.explain: Immunoglobulins are made by plasma cells, which are differentiated B cells. Hepatocytes make most other plasma proteins, but not antibodies.

test.q: Which enzyme cuts fibrinogen to start forming a clot?
test.explain: Thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides from fibrinogen, letting fibrin polymerize. Factor XIIIa acts afterward to cross-link the strands, and plasmin breaks clots down.

test.q: In nephrotic syndrome, the kidneys leak albumin into the urine. What is the most likely result?
choices: Swelling from fluid leaking into tissues
Jaundice from excess red cell breakdown
Bleeding from a lack of clotting factors
Dehydration from water lost in the urine
test.explain: Losing albumin lowers oncotic pressure, so fluid seeps into tissues and causes edema, often around the eyes and ankles.

test.q: On serum protein electrophoresis, a narrow spike in the gamma region suggests:
test.explain: A narrow M-spike means one clone is making one antibody, as in MGUS or myeloma. Chronic inflammation causes a broad polyclonal rise instead.

test.q: During acute inflammation, which protein level typically falls?
test.explain: Albumin is a negative acute phase reactant: IL-6 shifts the liver away from making it. Fibrinogen, CRP and haptoglobin rise.

test.q: Why can a strongly albumin-bound drug have a bigger effect when albumin is low?
choices: The drug is absorbed faster from the gut
The kidneys clear the drug more slowly
The drug binds more tightly to receptors
More of the drug circulates unbound
test.explain: Only the free, unbound fraction of a drug is active. With less albumin to bind it, a larger fraction is free.

test.q: Which organ makes albumin and fibrinogen?
test.explain: Hepatocytes in the liver synthesize most plasma proteins, except the immunoglobulins.

test.q: Immunoglobulins appear in the ___ fraction on serum protein electrophoresis.
test.explain: The bands run albumin, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta and gamma; antibodies sit in the gamma band.

test.q: Which plasma protein is converted by thrombin into the threads of a blood clot?
test.explain: Fibrinogen (factor I) is cleaved by thrombin into fibrin, which polymerizes into clot strands.

kidTest.q: What is plasma mostly made of?
kidTest.explain: Plasma is mostly water, with proteins and other helpers floating in it.

kidTest.q: What job does albumin do?
choices: Fights germs that get inside you
kidTest.explain: Albumin acts like a sponge that holds water in your blood vessels so you don't get puffy.

kidTest.q: Antibodies that fight germs belong to which protein group?
kidTest.explain: Some globulins are antibodies, the germ-fighters of the blood.

kidTest.q: What does fibrinogen help make when you get a cut?
kidTest.explain: Fibrinogen turns into sticky threads that make a net to plug the leak.

kidTest.q: Which body part is the factory that makes most blood proteins? l _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Your liver makes most of the proteins in plasma, like albumin and fibrinogen.

advancedTest.q: People with congenital analbuminemia have only mild edema. The best explanation is:
choices: Fibrinogen production rises enough to take over albumin's oncotic role
Higher globulins and lower tissue protein help keep the oncotic gradient
Their kidneys excrete extra sodium and water to prevent any fluid buildup
Their capillaries develop unusually tight junctions that stop fluid leaking
advancedTest.explain: What drives fluid back is the oncotic gradient, not albumin itself. Compensatory globulin rises and reduced interstitial protein partly preserve that gradient.

advancedTest.q: A hypoalbuminemic patient on a highly albumin-bound drug shows toxicity although the total drug level is in the usual range. The best explanation is:
choices: A larger unbound fraction makes the free level higher than total implies
The assay cross-reacts with globulins and so underestimates total drug levels
Low albumin directly raises the sensitivity of drug receptors in the tissues
Globulins bind the drug instead and deliver it more efficiently into tissues
advancedTest.explain: Total level = bound + free. With less albumin, the free (active) fraction rises even when the total looks normal, which is why free levels are measured.

advancedTest.q: Why does the erythrocyte sedimentation rate rise during an acute phase response?
choices: Antibodies break red cells into small fragments that settle more quickly
Rising albumin coats red cells and makes them denser and quicker to sink
Inflammatory cytokines swell red cells so that each one becomes heavier
Fibrinogen reduces red cell surface repulsion, promoting stacked rouleaux
advancedTest.explain: Fibrinogen lowers the zeta potential between red cells, so they stack into rouleaux that sediment faster. Albumin actually falls in inflammation and opposes rouleaux.

advancedTest.q: In the SAFE trial's traumatic brain injury subgroup, albumin resuscitation was linked to higher mortality. The proposed mechanism was:
choices: Dilution of fibrinogen, leading to expansion of intracranial bleeding
Raised intracranial pressure, possibly from hypotonic fluid
Allergic reactions to donor albumin, causing dangerous drops in pressure
Albumin binding of anticonvulsants, causing more post-traumatic seizures
advancedTest.explain: SAFE-TBI follow-up linked albumin to higher intracranial pressure, possibly because the 4% solution is mildly hypotonic, which is a key concern in neurosurgical patients.

lessons.title: Reading a Blood Smear: Normal Cell Morphology

levels.kid:
Have you ever spread butter very thin on toast? Scientists do something like that with blood. They put one tiny drop on a glass slide and smear it into a super-thin layer. Then they add pink and purple dyes and look through a microscope.

What do they see?
- **Red blood cells**: lots and lots of them! They are tiny round discs, pink with a pale middle, like a donut that forgot to make its hole.
- **White blood cells**: fewer and bigger, with a big purple center. There are five kinds, and each one has its own look.
- **Platelets**: tiny purple specks that help stop bleeding.

Reading a smear is like being a detective who checks blood one cell at a time. Each cell's shape and color are clues.
levels.hs:
A **peripheral blood smear** is a thin film of blood spread on a glass slide, stained, and examined under a microscope. Automated analyzers count cells quickly, but a trained eye can judge shapes and details that a machine may miss.

**Making it.** A drop of blood is placed near one end of a slide, and a second slide pushes it into a thin film. The film is thick where it started and thins out to a **feathered edge**. Cells are studied just behind that edge, where they lie side by side without overlapping, called the **monolayer**. The slide is colored with a **Wright-Giemsa stain**, which mixes an acidic pink dye (eosin) with basic blue-purple dyes.

**What normal looks like:**
- **Red blood cells (RBCs)**: round pink discs about 7-8 micrometers across, with a pale center (**central pallor**) about one third of the cell's width. A small lymphocyte's nucleus is about the same size, so it works as a built-in ruler.
- **White blood cells**, from most to least common: neutrophils (40-70%), lymphocytes (20-40%), monocytes (2-10%), eosinophils (1-4%), basophils (under 1%). Mnemonic: "Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas."
- **Platelets**: small purple fragments 2-3 micrometers across, with no nucleus.

Real example: a machine reports a low platelet count, but the smear shows platelets stuck together in clumps. The true count is probably normal, and the patient is spared needless worry and treatment.
levels.college:
Smear review follows a fixed routine so that nothing is skipped.

**Low power (10x).** Check smear quality, look for platelet clumps at the feathered edge, look for red cell stacking (**rouleaux**), and scan for rare abnormal cells. Then move to the monolayer and switch to high power or **oil immersion (100x)**.

**Red cells.** Judge size against a small lymphocyte nucleus (about 7 micrometers), color (normal central pallor is about one third of the diameter), and shape. Slightly larger, blue-gray cells show **polychromasia**: these are young reticulocytes that still contain ribosomal RNA. An exact reticulocyte count needs a supravital stain such as **new methylene blue**.

**White cells:**
- **Neutrophil** (12-15 micrometers): 2-5 nuclear lobes joined by thin chromatin strands, with pale lilac cytoplasm and fine granules. A **band** has a curved, unsegmented nucleus. Some neutrophils in females show a small "drumstick" (the Barr body).
- **Eosinophil**: usually bilobed nucleus, large refractile orange-red granules.
- **Basophil**: dark purple-black granules that often hide the nucleus.
- **Lymphocyte**: small forms (7-10 micrometers) have a dense round nucleus and a thin rim of sky-blue cytoplasm. Larger forms have more cytoplasm, sometimes with pink-purple (azurophilic) granules: these are **large granular lymphocytes** (NK cells and cytotoxic T cells).
- **Monocyte** (up to about 20 micrometers, the largest): folded or kidney-shaped nucleus with lacy chromatin, plentiful gray-blue cytoplasm, sometimes vacuoles.

**Platelets.** Count the average per oil field and multiply by roughly 20,000 to estimate platelets per microliter. About 7-20 per field is normal.

**Artifacts to recognize:**
- Thick area: overlapping cells and false rouleaux.
- Thin tip of the feathered edge: flattened red cells lose their pallor and mimic spherocytes, and large white cells pile up there.
- Slow drying or old samples: crenated, spiky red cells.
- EDTA tube: in some people platelets clump, so the analyzer count is falsely low.

Always convert percentages to **absolute counts** (percentage times total WBC). A "high" lymphocyte percentage can simply reflect too few neutrophils.
levels.phd:
**The Romanowsky effect.** Wright and Giemsa stains rely on **azure B**, an oxidation product of methylene blue, together with **eosin Y**. Cationic azure B binds anionic phosphate groups in DNA and RNA, so ribosome-rich cytoplasm turns blue ("basophilic"). Anionic eosin binds cationic proteins, so hemoglobin and the arginine-rich major basic protein in eosinophil granules turn orange-pink ("acidophilic"). The purple of chromatin is not simple dye mixing. It comes from an azure B-eosin complex that forms on DNA, and this needs the right buffer pH, typically about 6.8. If the buffer is too acidic, eosin dominates: red cells look bright red and nuclei look pale. If it is too alkaline, red cells turn gray-blue and eosinophil granules look dull. Neutrophil specific granules take up neither dye strongly, which gave the cell its name. Basophil granules, rich in sulfated heparin, stain **metachromatically** and are partly water-soluble, so they can wash out.

**Red cell geometry.** The biconcave disc is about 7.5-8 micrometers across and about 2-2.5 micrometers thick at the rim, thinning to about 1 micrometer centrally. Central pallor is the optical signature of this biconcavity. Its size tracks hemoglobin concentration and surface-to-volume ratio.

**Counting statistics.** A manual differential is a binomial sample. Rümke's 1960 analysis showed how wide the confidence limits are: on a 100-cell count, a true 5% population has a 95% interval of roughly 1.6-11%. Rare cells such as basophils are therefore estimated very imprecisely. Counting 200 or 400 cells narrows the interval, and analyzers sampling thousands of cells are far more precise for normal populations. Their weakness is accuracy with abnormal cells, not precision.

**Nuclear segmentation.** Lobe number rises as a neutrophil matures, with a mean of about three. The classic upper limit of normal is no cell with six or more lobes and fewer than 5% with five lobes.

**Controversy: band counts.** Bands are defined by nuclear shape, yet observers disagree widely on where a band ends and a segmented cell begins. Studies show poor interobserver reproducibility and little diagnostic value beyond the total neutrophil count. For that reason, many laboratories now report bands together with segmented neutrophils.
levels.expert:
**When to look.** Most complete blood counts never reach a microscope. The International Consensus Group for Hematology Review (Barnes and colleagues, 2005) proposed 41 criteria for smear review, including first-time abnormal counts, analyzer flags, and unexplained delta changes. Laboratories adapt these to their own analyzers and patient populations.

**Digital morphology.** Systems such as CellaVision photograph cells and preclassify them with trained algorithms. A technologist then verifies each class. Deep-learning classifiers now perform well on normal leukocytes, but rare, dysplastic and degenerating cells remain hard, and validation must include local staining variation.

**Spurious results the smear corrects:**
- **EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia** (about 0.1% of people): autoantibodies recognize epitopes on platelet GPIIb/IIIa exposed when EDTA removes calcium. The smear shows clumps or **platelet satellitism** (platelets ringing neutrophils). Recollect in citrate or heparin and report that count. In a patient awaiting neurosurgery, this prevents a cancelled operation or an unnecessary platelet transfusion.
- **Cold agglutinins**: red cell agglutinates on the smear explain a falsely low RBC count with spuriously high MCV and MCHC. Warming the sample corrects the indices.
- **Storage artifact**: after about a day in EDTA, red cells crenate, neutrophil nuclei swell and fragment, and monocytes vacuolate. These changes mimic real disease.
- **Smudge cells**: fragile lymphocytes ruptured by spreading. Adding albumin before making the smear preserves them.

**Reference intervals are population-specific.** Many people of African or Middle Eastern ancestry carry the Duffy-null phenotype (ACKR1). They have a lower but healthy neutrophil count, now termed **Duffy-null associated neutrophil count**. Applying generic limits leads to needless marrow biopsies and to exclusion from clinical trials.

**Age matters.** Newborn red cells are larger, and a few nucleated red cells are normal in the first days of life. Lymphocytes outnumber neutrophils from about the end of the first week until roughly age 4-5. A lymphocyte-predominant smear in a toddler is usually normal.

**Open questions.** How should AI-assisted morphology be regulated and audited? Which flags truly need human review? Can quantitative imaging, such as red cell shape metrics, replace subjective grading?

keyPoints: A blood smear is a thin stained film read in the monolayer just behind the feathered edge
Wright-Giemsa: eosin stains hemoglobin and eosinophil granules; azure dyes stain nucleic acids
Normal RBCs are 7-8 micrometers with central pallor about one third of the diameter
WBC frequency: neutrophils > lymphocytes > monocytes > eosinophils > basophils
Platelets per oil field x about 20,000 gives a rough platelet count
Recognize artifacts: feathered-edge false spherocytes, drying crenation, EDTA platelet clumping

test.q: Where on a blood smear should cell morphology be judged?
choices: Along the side margins of the slide
At the tip of the feathered edge
test.explain: The monolayer just behind the feathered edge has cells side by side without overlap. The thick area overlaps cells, and the thin tip flattens them.

test.q: In a normal red blood cell on a smear, the central pallor is:
choices: Absent in healthy mature red cells
About two thirds of the cell's width
About one third of the cell's width
test.explain: Normal central pallor occupies roughly one third of the diameter and reflects the biconcave disc shape.

test.q: In a healthy adult, which white cell is the most common on a smear?
test.explain: Neutrophils make up about 40-70% of white cells in adults. Lymphocytes come second, at about 20-40%.

test.q: Which cell has a usually bilobed nucleus and large orange-red granules?
test.explain: Eosinophil granules contain cationic major basic protein, which binds eosin and turns orange-red. Basophil granules are dark purple-black instead.

test.q: Which is the largest normal white cell, with a folded kidney-shaped nucleus and gray-blue cytoplasm?
test.explain: Monocytes reach about 20 micrometers and have a folded nucleus with lacy chromatin and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm.

test.q: Why do readers compare red cells with the nucleus of a small lymphocyte?
choices: It reveals the cell's hemoglobin content
It shows how well the stain worked
It estimates the overall platelet count
It gives a built-in size reference
test.explain: A small lymphocyte nucleus is about 7 micrometers, close to a normal red cell, so it serves as a ruler for judging red cell size.

test.q: On a Wright-stained smear, slightly large blue-gray red cells (polychromasia) are:
choices: Old red cells about to be removed
Red cells that dried too slowly
Young red cells with leftover RNA
test.explain: Polychromatic cells are reticulocytes. Their residual ribosomal RNA takes up the basic azure dye and gives a bluish tint.

test.q: A smear shows about 12 platelets per oil-immersion field. Using a factor of about 20,000, the estimate is:
test.explain: 12 x 20,000 = 240,000 per microliter, which falls within the normal range.

test.q: An analyzer reports a low platelet count, but the smear shows large platelet clumps. This most likely reflects:
choices: Clumping caused by the EDTA tube
Destruction of platelets in the spleen
test.explain: In some people platelets clump in EDTA, so the machine counts clumps as single cells or misses them. This is pseudothrombocytopenia, not a true low count.

test.q: Which acidic (anionic) dye in Wright-Giemsa stain colors hemoglobin pink-orange?
test.explain: Anionic eosin binds cationic proteins such as hemoglobin and major basic protein. The basic azure dyes stain nucleic acids blue-purple instead.

test.q: A normal mature neutrophil has 2 to 5 nuclear ___ joined by thin chromatin strands.
test.explain: Segmented neutrophils have 2-5 lobes. Six or more lobes is beyond the normal limit.

test.q: Name the supravital stain used to count reticulocytes accurately.
test.explain: New methylene blue precipitates residual RNA in living reticulocytes, so they can be counted precisely.

kidTest.q: How is blood spread out to look at it under a microscope?
choices: A very thin layer on glass
Mixed into a glass of water
A thick blob in a cup
kidTest.explain: The blood is smeared very thin on a glass slide, like butter on toast.

kidTest.q: What do red blood cells look like on a smear?
choices: Round discs with a pale middle
kidTest.explain: Red cells look like tiny pink donuts without a hole: round with a pale middle.

kidTest.q: Which cells are bigger and have a big purple center?
kidTest.explain: White blood cells are bigger and have a large purple center called the nucleus.

kidTest.q: Why do scientists add pink and purple dyes to the smear?
choices: To help us see cell parts
kidTest.explain: The dyes color the different parts of each cell so they are easy to see.

kidTest.q: Tiny purple specks that help stop bleeding are called p _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Platelets are tiny cell pieces that help plug cuts.

advancedTest.q: Why is a 100-cell manual differential a poor estimate of the basophil percentage?
choices: Basophils are destroyed by EDTA within minutes
Sampling error is large when few cells are counted
Basophils hide among red cells in the thick zone
Basophils resemble small lymphocytes on staining
advancedTest.explain: A differential is a binomial sample. As Rümke showed, confidence intervals are very wide for rare populations on a 100-cell count. The other options are not the main problem.

advancedTest.q: A trainee reports many spherocytes, but only in the thin tip of the feathered edge. Normal red cells are seen in the monolayer. The most likely explanation is:
choices: An artifact from reading too far out
advancedTest.explain: At the thin tip, red cells are flattened and lose central pallor, mimicking spherocytes. True spherocytes would also appear in the monolayer.

advancedTest.q: A well, non-bleeding patient awaiting surgery has a very low analyzer platelet count. The smear shows platelets ringing neutrophils, and a citrate sample gives a normal count. Best next step:
advancedTest.explain: Platelet satellitism and a normal citrate count point to EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia. The true count is normal, so transfusion, biopsy or treatment would be inappropriate.

advancedTest.q: On a Wright-stained smear, red cells appear bright red and nuclei look pale and washed out. The most likely cause is:
choices: The staining buffer was too acidic
The staining buffer was too alkaline
The smear was made too thick
advancedTest.explain: Acidic pH favors eosin binding and weakens the azure B-eosin complex that makes chromatin purple. An alkaline buffer would make red cells gray-blue instead.
